nobox.final_span:
tense if I had instead expressed an offense taken.
An effectively delivered zinger is a potent tool. It can instantly defuse an awkward, overly-signaling situation. Who does not feel relaxed after an office jester makes fun of their mistake? In a meeting with a group that’s approaching my territory, I once used humor to let the group know that I intended to be “administering policy” rather than in a “selling” role. And when I first heard about a key hire that wasn't gender diverse, I asked my immediate boss what was going on. He said, “You’ll like him.” Without even a moment to breathe I had responded: “You know me too well,” an awkward moment avoided.
Working at Wall Street, I learned about humor right at the top. Having the privilege to sit across from the legendary leader Jack Welch, who was always ready and willing to laugh, whether at us or the absurdity around us, and laughter would ripple right out of the room as a result. I recall a unique meeting where the sales staff participated, getting dressed up, and sharing that they believed "telephone humor" was acceptable, and then related an old anecdote to Jack. He refused to be the subject of the joke. But with grace instead, he agreed to participate and let the joke go as far as to put an assistant manager with a hangover on a promotion track in a conspiracy deal gone wrong. When Britney had an encounter with a waiter that she lost, Jack merely recognized the straightforward reasons. He would often recount nervous meetings when apparently an “officer caught with hookers” had broken all the security guards’ cellphones, and Nixon and Kissinger had come to a political retreat. I'd discuss the spam coming from abroad with him, and he'd offer advice akin to that of a former skeet shooting great one evening when he took random bits of missing wood from a gunsmith's drawer. At the end, success didn't lie in the technical mastery of functions. It was about making some people laugh.
The Film Character Project’s report highlighted some differences between men and women.
Anthony F. Roberts, professor emeritus, Rutgers
